hook.line: Tomás's new day starts at five and ends early, because the bakery won't wait. To tell anyone about your day in Spanish, you need a small word that points back at you. You've been using one since day one: *me llamo*.
hook.es: Ya me voy. ¡Uy, se me hizo tarde!
hook.en: I'm off now. Oh no, I'm running late!

examples.es: Me voy a la cama a las diez.
examples.en: I go to bed at ten.
How are you feeling today? (to a friend)

examples.es: Vale se va a Medellín el viernes.
examples.en: Vale is leaving for Medellín on Friday.

examples.es: Nos encontramos en el café a las ocho.
examples.en: We meet at the café at eight.
You look like your grandmother. (to a friend)

rule:
Some Spanish verbs travel with a little word that points back at whoever is doing them. It changes with the person:

*me*: I
*te*: you (a friend)
*se*: he, she, you (formal)
*nos*: we
*se*: they, you all

So *me voy* is I'm off, *se va* is she's off, *nos vamos* is we're off. English usually has no "myself" here, so don't look for one: *me siento bien* is just I feel well.

The little word goes right before the verb, and *no* goes before both: *No me siento bien.* After *voy a*, you can glue it to the end instead: *Voy a irme* or *Me voy a ir*, same thing.

This is how a whole routine gets told: *me levanto* (I get up), *me ducho* (I shower), *me acuesto* (I go to bed). You'll get those verbs later this week; they work exactly like *me voy*.
smallPrint: Teachers call these reflexive verbs, and *me*, *te*, *se*, *nos* reflexive pronouns. In the dictionary they end in *-se*: *irse*, *sentirse*, *llamarse*.

readAndPick.es: Se va a la cama temprano.
options: You go to bed early. (to a friend)
You look like your mum. (to a friend)

readAndPick.es: Me encuentro con Vale en el parque.
options: We meet Vale in the park.
Vale meets her friend in the park.
I meet Vale in the park.

yourTurn.prompt: Fill the gap with *me* or *se*, then type the whole sentence: "*Vale ___ va a las seis.*" (Vale leaves at six.)
yourTurn.answer: Vale se va a las seis.
yourTurn.why: Vale is she, and she takes *se*.

yourTurn.prompt: Fill the gap with *te* or *se*. You're asking a friend: "*¿Cómo ___ sientes?*"
yourTurn.why: A friend is *tú*, so the little word is *te*, matching *sientes*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: We're leaving early.
yourTurn.why: We is *nos* plus *vamos*: both point at the same people.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I don't feel well.
yourTurn.why: *No* comes first, then *me*, then the verb.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about Vale and Mariana: "*Me voy a la cama a las diez.*"
yourTurn.answer: Se van a la cama a las diez.
accept: Vale y Mariana se van a la cama a las diez.
yourTurn.why: They take *se*, and the verb takes the *they* ending: *van*.
*No* goes in front of the little word, never between it and the verb.

yourTurn.prompt: Say the same thing with the little word glued to the end: "*Me voy a ir temprano.*"
yourTurn.why: After *voy a*, the *me* can join the end of *ir*: *irme*.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a stranger you call *usted*: Are you leaving?
yourTurn.why: *Usted* shares *se* and *va* with he and she.

pitfalls.why: Almost. *Se* is for he, she and they; for I, it's *me*.
The little word and the ending both have to say we: *nos vamos*.
The little word goes before *voy* or on the end of *ir*, never in the middle.
Feeling well needs its little word. Without *me*, *siento* is I feel something, or I'm sorry.

personal: Tell someone about your evening: what time you go to bed (*me voy a la cama a las...*) and how you feel today (*me siento...*).
